note:
v1, IN THE TIME OF (track nine, whole-song skeleton). The drum pulse never leaves 84. Two guitars teach seven strokes slowly: open F, mute, mute, answer, mute, answer, mute. Each seven bars the space between strokes shrinks: one per beat, then two, three, four, five and six. Before seven, the head of the cell meets a quarter only once in seven beats. The two pitch answers alternate; the articulation repeats in seven strokes, the pitches in fourteen.
At five and six (1:20–2:00) the guitars thin to two and a short F4 tap marks each cell head. Its two custom wavetable frames come from the riff: harmonics 1/4/6 from the open notes, 2/3/5/7 from the muted ones. At 2:00 the tap gives its job to the kick and bass: seven guitar strokes now fit one quarter, six guitars play them, and the rhythm section walks. At 2:40 the slow seven strokes return as chords. 3:06 written, 3:11 with the tail.

WHAT I MEASURED (I cannot listen): 81.27 / 82.24 on seeds 0 / 11. Both files −10.0 LUFS, −1.29 dBTP. At the lock the band steps up 2.0 LU, against 0.5 in the first draft. I cut the kick from all 392 fast strokes to the 56 cell heads (checked against the guitar timestamps). The mono mix in the first three bars of the lock is 2.7 dB short at 60–120 Hz and 2.9 over at 120–250 vs the reference records. I kept the quarter-note kick rather than putting the roll back for low end. The tap at −9 dB gain sits 8.4 / 8.9 dB under the stereo mix on its attacks in the samples at 1:30 / 1:40; its first level put it over 11 dB under. The score's off-grid share reads zero despite the checked note grid; that measures the mixed accents, not the written spacing.
WHAT I CANNOT KNOW: whether the kit lets you feel the same beat at every speed; whether the landing feels heavier or just busier; whether you recognise the opening when it comes back. No new card: the existing listening page can be answered in its own time.

note:
v2, PICKED AND KEYED (palette round as drawn, 1:00–1:20). At four notes to the beat the seven-stroke riff has two pitches trying to speak between the low F strokes. In v1 four distorted guitars played both pitches together. Here the guitars leave those two places empty: a baritone guitar on the left picks the first note an octave up; a clavinet on the right keys the other, two octaves up. Eight cells later, at 1:10, they swap who asks and who answers. Their sides do not swap. The bass keeps the original pitches; the kick, snare and cell heads stay where they were. At 1:20 the pair stops and the existing tap marks the fives. Nothing added to the 2:00 lock.

- Full song: http://pocket4:8790/clips/chirper-zero-inthetimeof-v2-full.mp3

Every other track besides the four affected guitars is note-identical to v1; the only edits to those guitars are at the 32 hook times. note:
v4, FOUR UNDER THREE (section round, window 3). The guitars are still playing triplets, but the drummer starts grouping them in fours a few bars before the band changes speed. From 0:45.7 to 1:00 the foot closes the hi-hat on four quarters while the sticks mark every fourth guitar stroke: three accents per bar against four foot taps. For two bars the ride bell has all three and the snare keeps the familiar backbeat. Then bell–snare–snare, snare–bell–snare, and finally the snare plays all three, rising in strength. At 1:00 the ordinary backbeat returns under four guitar strokes per beat. No new guitar line, no change of tempo. The kick, bass and the seven-note cell are untouched throughout.

note:
v7, COUNT THE STROKES (section w7, the A-flat change inside the lock). By 2:00 the riff has got as fast as it is going to get. At 2:23 it counts up a second time without speeding up: the six guitars play the head alone, then two strokes of the seven, then three, until they play the whole cell. Then they start taking strokes away from the head, not the tail. Each answer comes in one slot later against the bass and kick until only the last pickup is left, then there is a beat with no guitar attack. All seven strokes come back on the next kick. No guitarist, drum or effect is added. Every surviving stroke has its v6 pitch, gate, velocity and time.

note:
Whole-song draw, DOWN THROUGH EVERY SPEED (2:35–2:40). The song climbed one speed at a time for two minutes and then left its top speed in a single cut. Now the last seven beats of the lock hold seven strokes, then six, five, four, three, two and one, and the slow chords at 2:40 are simply the next speed down. Seven beats, 28 strokes: exactly four of the seven-stroke cells, so the riff is never cut short; each cell is longer than the last (1, 1.2, 1.55, 3.25 beats) and the next head is the first slow chord. The bass and kick do at each speed what they did in that part of the song (on the beat at seven; head and two answers from six to three; every stroke at two and one). China and backbeat keep 84. The single notes thicken on the way down (answers as fifth-and-octave chords from five to the beat, mutes from three), so the chords at 2:40 are already under the hand. In A-flat the last cell reads A-flat, B, D and the next head is F: minor thirds up to the home chord. The old two-beat tom fill is gone; the gears are the fill. Changed: six guitars, bass and kick in beats 218–224; six tom and two snare fill notes removed. Nothing else.

note:
v13, PIPES AT ONE TO THE BEAT (palette). THE ADDITION: a pipe organ, the library's organ-pipe, on a new track 'wind'. No other song on the record has one. Each speed on the way up had a guest (open hat at two, ride bell at three, baritone and clavinet at four, the tap at five and six); the return to one had none. Only at one stroke to the beat does a note last long enough to be held, so from 2:40 to 2:50 the organ holds what the six guitars strike: the open F for its three beats, then each answer through the muted stroke after it. note:
v14, FIVE, COUNTED BY HAND (section w4, 1:20.0–1:30.0, the first two turns of the fives; my last note called them the least worked stretch). 'Five in the time of four' is how a musician says a quintuplet; in North India it is a tala. A TABLA plays jhaptal, the ten-beat cycle, at five strokes to the beat: dhin na | dhin dhin na, tin na | dhin dhin na. Its two-and-three fall inside every beat of the kit. Its ten strokes last two beats, so the bass drum of the pair sounds on one and three and is left out on two and four, where the snare is. Three things now turn at once: the kit in four, the tabla in ten, the riff in seven; the riff's head and its tap land on a different bol each time (first, third, fifth, second, fourth). The last two beats are a tihai, the thrice-said cadence: te re dha three times with a stroke's rest between, so a dha every fourth stroke of five. Its last dha is the beat where the tap begins its tune (v6): the five places in the beat are counted by a drum, then the tap gives each a pitch. The kit, guitars, bass and tap do not change. New sound: it-tabla, the library tabla-kit (no other song on the record uses it), treble drum on F4, bass drum on the riff's F2.
LISTEN FOR: 1:20, a hand drum under the guitars, five to the beat, its low stroke on one and three; at 1:28 three dhas and it is gone as the tap starts its tune. v13 then v14, 1:16.6–1:33.2: http://pocket4:8790/clips/three-c10-t9-v14-five-by-hand-ab.mp3 ; the tabla with the kit, bass and tap, no guitars: http://pocket4:8790/clips/three-c10-t9-v14-five-by-hand-hands.mp3 . note:
v15, THE SLOW TUNE UNDER THE FAST ONE (whole-song round; 2:00.0–2:22.9, the lock on F). The song opens with the riff at one note to the beat and arrives, two minutes later, at seven to the beat, where the bass and the kick only walked: a low F on every beat for 32 beats. The walk is now the OPENING. Under the lock the bass plays the riff at one note to the beat again, as the two guitars did at 0:00 (F F F A flat F B F, then F F F G flat F C F), while six guitars play those same seven notes inside every one of its beats: seven in the time of one, over one, the song's first speed and its last at once. The bass still strikes every beat with the kick; only nine of its 32 notes leave F. A slow cell is seven beats and the lock is 32, so the fifth cell gets as far as its first answer, A flat, on the last beat before the band moves up to A flat: the note the riff has always answered with is the key the song goes to, and the bass is there one beat early (at 0:35 it is the last to turn; here the first). No new sound, no new part, no stroke moved.
